lesson.title: Eating Your Greens: Plants, Herbivores, and an Evolutionary Arms Race
lesson.summary: Herbivory, animals consuming plant or algal tissue, is a plus-minus interspecific interaction that, like predation, has driven a long-running evolutionary back and forth between plant defenses and herbivore counter-adaptations.
lesson.body:
Herbivory is the consumption of plant or algal tissue by an animal, and it is one of the most widespread interspecific interactions on Earth, given how much of the planet's living matter is plant material. Like predation, it fits the plus-minus pattern: the herbivore gains nutrition, while the plant is harmed. But herbivory usually differs from predation in one important respect: eating part of a plant does not necessarily kill it the way a predator killing its prey does. A grazing animal that eats grass, or an insect that chews part of a leaf, may damage the plant without ending its life, though severe or repeated herbivory certainly can kill a plant, and consuming seeds is functionally closer to predation on that individual seed.

Herbivores take many different forms depending on what and how they eat. Grazers feed on low growing vegetation such as grasses, bison and zebra among them. Browsers feed on the leaves and twigs of shrubs and trees, giraffes and deer being familiar examples. Seed predators consume seeds specifically, and sap feeders like aphids draw nutrient rich fluid directly from plant tissue without necessarily consuming solid plant matter at all.

Because being eaten carries a real fitness cost, plants have evolved a wide range of defenses against herbivory, and herbivores have evolved counter-adaptations in response, producing a coevolutionary arms race much like the one seen between predators and prey. Plant defenses include physical deterrents such as thorns, spines, tough or hairy leaf surfaces, and silica embedded in grass tissue that wears down herbivore teeth, as well as chemical deterrents: a large and diverse group of compounds called secondary metabolites, including alkaloids, tannins, and terpenoids, that can taste bad, interfere with digestion, or be outright toxic to would-be herbivores.

A well documented example of this arms race involves milkweed, which produces toxic compounds called cardiac glycosides that make most herbivores avoid it. Monarch butterfly caterpillars, however, have evolved the ability to feed on milkweed despite these toxins, and remarkably they sequester the compounds in their own tissues rather than simply neutralizing them, which makes the caterpillars, and later the adult butterflies, toxic or distasteful to their own predators in turn. This is a clear case of a herbivore not just overcoming a plant defense but repurposing it for its own protection.

Herbivores have evolved their own counter-adaptations beyond tolerating specific toxins, including enzymes that detoxify particular plant chemicals and, notably, specialized digestive systems. Many mammalian herbivores, cows and deer among them, host large communities of microorganisms in specialized stomach chambers that can break down cellulose, the tough structural carbohydrate in plant cell walls that the animal's own digestive enzymes cannot process on their own.

Herbivory connects back to several earlier concepts in this unit. It can act as a limiting factor on plant populations, and a food supply limiting factor on herbivore populations in turn, and its intensity often scales with herbivore density, one more example of a density-dependent pressure. It is also worth noting, with appropriate caution, that the relationship between plants and herbivory is not purely destructive: in some grassland ecosystems, moderate grazing appears to be associated with maintaining plant community health or diversity rather than simply degrading it, though the details of when and why that holds are an active area of ecological study rather than a simple universal rule.
